The transformative potential of solid-state transformers90 min40 insights2026-11-11
▶ Watch on YouTube
Nphase co-founder Ragu Balure explains how solid state transformers built from ~1,000 modular 5 kW GaN power converters can replace copper-and-iron transformers, with AI data centers moving to 800 V DC (pilots 2027, ramp 2028) and grid batteries as the beachhead, utility-scale solar next, and the 60-million-unit neighborhood distribution transformer fleet as the long-term prize. He argues semiconductor cost curves will reach parity in 3-5 years, while durability (10-year warranty vs 50-year iron) and utility conservatism remain the key hurdles.
Why the transformer is due for disruption · 6SST technology: semiconductors replace copper and iron · 8Data centers and 800V DC as the beachhead · 8Utility-scale solar and BESS applications · 4Nphase scale, track record and SST economics · 7Distribution grid prize, utilities and policy · 7
Why the transformer is due for disruption 6
Conventional copper-and-iron line-frequency (60 Hz) transformers have barely changed in a century; they are cheap, reliable and efficient but 'dumb', and the US currently cannot make them fast enough, with multi-year lead times.
data_point🗣 David Robertsconviction: hightransformersUS grid
So what: Transformer shortage is a structural bottleneck for grid buildout; supply-constrained incumbents and any credible substitute both benefit.
“Right now, the US can't make them fast enough. It takes years to get one.” ▶ 1:05
Conventional transformers can only do AC-in/AC-out at fixed voltage ratios: they cannot convert AC to DC, cannot handle DC, and are blind to harmonics and noise created by fluctuating loads like data centers.
framework🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: hightransformersdata centers
So what: Defines the functional gap SSTs fill: DC-native loads/sources and power-quality management are the wedge use cases.
Bidirectional power flow from rooftop solar, home batteries and bidirectional EV chargers means the grid must add intelligence (monitoring and control of power flow) at every node rather than rely only on brute-force generation additions.
thesis🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highrooftop solarbatteriesEV chargersNphase
So what: Supports demand for grid-edge power electronics, VPPs and smart distribution equipment as DER penetration rises.
“So it's no longer a unidirectional power flow. Now the power flow has become completely birectional.” ▶ 9:53
Power electronics have taken over phones, cars and nearly everything else but not the grid, mainly because of utility institutional conservatism around reliability combined with the recent arrival of enabling compute and wide-bandgap devices.
causal🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumpower electronicsutilities
So what: Adoption pace is gated by institutions more than physics; watch utility pilots and standards as leading indicators.
Roughly 60 million neighborhood pole-top/pad-mount distribution transformers exist in the US, and the host has read that around half are near the end of their rated life, creating a massive replacement wave.
data_point🗣 David Robertsconviction: mediumdistribution transformersUS grid
So what: A looming replacement cycle is the largest addressable market for SSTs and a demand tailwind for conventional transformer makers in the interim.
The host warns that the current transformer shortage is prompting a surge of conventional transformer manufacturing, risking a lock-in of decades-lived dumb transformers before SSTs are ready.
thesis🗣 David Robertsconviction: mediumtransformerssolid state transformers
So what: Near-term orders likely still go to conventional transformers; SST penetration of distribution may be delayed by this installed-base lock-in.
SST technology: semiconductors replace copper and iron 8
A solid state transformer uses semiconductors (wide-bandgap silicon carbide or gallium nitride) to chop power at high frequency (10 kHz to hundreds of kHz vs 60 Hz), shrinking the magnetic component and enabling any-voltage-to-any-voltage, AC or DC, fully bidirectional conversion with monitoring and control.
framework🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highsolid state transformerssilicon carbidegallium nitride
So what: Core technology mechanism; wide-bandgap semiconductor suppliers are direct beneficiaries of SST adoption.
Ragu Balure argues semiconductor-and-software-based products keep compounding cost, reliability and performance improvements, whereas copper and iron costs asymptote because materials are bought by weight.
thesis🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highsemiconductorscopperNphase
So what: Framework for betting on power-electronics substitutes over materials-intensive incumbents across clean energy hardware.
“copper and iron is copper and iron I mean I buy them by weight” ▶ 17:36
The combination of cheap compute and the availability of wide-bandgap devices is what has made solid state transformers viable today, per Ragu Balure.
causal🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highwide band gapsilicon carbidegallium nitride
So what: Wide-bandgap supply-chain maturity is the enabling factor to track for SST commercialization timelines.
Nphase's SST builds a 5 MVA transformer from about 1,000 modular 5 kW power converters, analogous to how data centers scale by adding GPUs tied together (e.g. Nvidia NVLink72), while others use ~100 kW building blocks.
framework🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highNphaseNvidiaNVLink72GPUs
So what: Modular architecture lets SST capacity scale linearly and leverages high-volume electronics manufacturing; a key differentiator versus monolithic SST designs.
Nphase's SST modules contain almost no copper (transformer core weighing hundreds of grams per 5 kW module), with silicone potting the largest weight contributor, shifting supply chains to standard surface-mount PCB manufacturing.
data_point🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumNphasecopper
So what: SSTs reduce exposure to copper constraints that limit conventional transformer and grid buildout.
Nphase chose gallium nitride over silicon carbide (moving roughly 10 years ago) because GaN-on-silicon allows higher switching frequencies, simpler manufacturing with larger ingots, and bidirectional GaN on a single die versus two dies for silicon carbide.
contrarian🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highNphasegallium nitridesilicon carbide
So what: Most SST competitors use silicon carbide; a GaN-based architecture is a differentiated bet that could shift wide-bandgap demand mix.
“Silicon carbide is the second hardest material in the world” ▶ 40:10
Ragu Balure argues that GaN is effectively a commodity and that, because Nphase uses only a thin epitaxial GaN layer on silicon, it has no material exposure to Chinese gallium supply concerns.
contrarian🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumgallium nitrideChinaNphase
So what: Counter to the consensus worry about China gallium controls; investors should verify GaN supply-chain resilience independently.
“we are not subject to any GAN supply chain concerns” ▶ 42:55
Nphase's control architecture is single-stage, 250-500 kHz switching with predictive control computed on its own custom ASIC (five ASIC generations, nine inverter generations), plus soft switching that minimizes harmonics and EMI.
data_point🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumNphaseASIC
So what: Proprietary silicon and control IP form Nphase's moat claim; fast response time also underpins its battery-savings pitch in data centers.
Data centers and 800V DC as the beachhead 8
AI training loads swing from 10% to 100% about five times per second, and SSTs plus batteries are needed to keep these fluctuations from being reflected back onto utility grids and rotating machines.
causal🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highdata centersAI trainingbatteriesutilities
So what: Load-smoothing equipment (SSTs, batteries) becomes a required spend for AI data center interconnection.
Rack power densities have climbed from about 30 kW to 150 kW to 250 kW today, with 1 MW racks being discussed; at 50 V a 1 MW rack would need 20,000 amps, making legacy low-voltage DC delivery infeasible.
data_point🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highdata centersserver racks
So what: Rising rack density forces a power-architecture overhaul inside data centers, creating a new equipment market.
Data centers are pushing toward 800 V DC in the white space (borrowed from EV DC fast-charging voltages), which cuts current to servers by roughly 18-20x and dramatically reduces copper and losses; the electrical code limit is 1,500 V DC.
thesis🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highdata centers800 volts DCEV charging
So what: 800 V DC adoption is the key catalyst for SSTs and DC power equipment suppliers; track hyperscaler announcements and standards.
Ragu Balure expects 800 V DC data center pilots in 2027 and deployments ramping in 2028 (possibly first deployments in late 2027), with quick adoption for any company delivering viable SSTs.
prediction🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highdata centerssolid state transformers800 volts DC
So what: Sets a concrete timeline: SST revenue inflection would be 2028+ for data centers.
“2027 you should expect pilots at 800 volts DC and then deployments in 2028” ▶ 52:58
An SST converting directly from 34,500 V AC medium voltage to 800 V DC can eliminate the transformer, PCS, double-conversion UPS and multiple downstream conversion stages, with estimated efficiency gains of about 4.5-5%.
data_point🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumsolid state transformersUPSdata centers
So what: Threatens incumbent UPS and multi-stage power-chain equipment vendors while improving data center economics.
Because data centers are power-constrained, a ~5% efficiency gain can be redeployed as ~5% more GPUs, raising revenue and tokens per watt rather than just saving energy.
causal🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumGPUshyperscalersdata centers
So what: Frames SST value in revenue terms for hyperscalers, supporting willingness to pay a premium.
Nphase pitches that its fast-response SSTs can let data centers rely on a distant 2-4 hour battery energy storage system (e.g. ~4 GWh, 30+ acres, a quarter mile away for a gigawatt campus) instead of per-rack battery backup units, freeing up to ~50% of side-rack space for compute.
thesis🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: exploratoryNphaseBESSbattery backup unitsdata centers
So what: If validated, reduces demand for in-rack BBUs and increases demand for utility-scale co-located BESS.
Hyperscalers are the first SST market because they have money and an urgent need for speed, mirroring how many clean energy technologies use deep-pocketed early adopters to fund early deployment and ride down the cost curve.
framework🗣 David Robertsconviction: mediumhyperscalerssolid state transformers
So what: Data center demand is the funding engine for SST cost reduction; later markets depend on its success.

SSTs placed in front of grid-scale batteries replace the power control system plus medium-voltage transformer with a single device, so Nphase plans to address data center and BESS markets almost simultaneously.
thesis🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumNphaseBESSsolid state transformers
So what: BESS integrators and PCS/transformer suppliers face a potential single-device substitute.
The US utility-scale PV market is estimated at 30-40 GW for 2027, with global markets larger, representing the next big SST opportunity after data centers and batteries.
data_point🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumutility-scale solar
So what: Sizes the second SST market; displaces central inverters plus step-up transformers.
Nphase oversizes its SSTs by about 6% (roughly 60 extra 5 kW modules in a 5 MVA unit), which Ragu Balure says could raise PV power-conversion reliability enough to move from typical 5-year warranties toward potentially 20-year warranties, a 3-4x improvement.
prediction🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: exploratoryNphaseutility-scale solar

anecdote🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: exploratoryNphaserobotics
So what: Could cut O&M costs and regulatory/training burden for field service if delivered.

Distribution grid prize, utilities and policy 7
The long-term prize for SSTs is the neighborhood distribution transformer, which Ragu Balure calls a necessity rather than a nice-to-have given bidirectional distributed energy, but proving reliability comes before cost in that market.
thesis🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highdistribution transformersutilitiessolid state transformers
So what: The largest TAM is the slowest to adopt; reliability proof in data centers and PV is the gating step.
Ragu Balure says Nphase is having more discussions with utilities about SSTs than expected and adoption could be faster than people think, though he knows of no US utility deploying SSTs on pole tops yet.
contrarian🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: lowNphaseutilities
So what: Watch for first utility distribution pilots as a signal the bigger market is opening.
SSTs interconnecting front-of-meter PV, BESS, data centers and fast DC charging at 34.5 kV or 13.8 kV will give grid operators firsthand experience with SST behavior, building the confidence needed for neighborhood deployment.
causal🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumutilitiesBESSdata centers
So what: Behind-the-meter and front-of-meter installs serve as a de facto pilot program for distribution adoption.
Solid state transformers are intrinsically current-limited, which Ragu Balure sees as an advantage for fault handling: with rate-of-change-of-current detection and emerging solid state breakers, faults can be isolated without dumping 100,000-amp surges.
contrarian🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumsolid state transformerssolid state breakers
So what: Complementary demand for solid state circuit breakers; protection-scheme redesign is a hurdle for utilities.
Ragu Balure argues cyber risk from software-controlled grid devices is solvable, citing device birth certificates at manufacture, segregation of safety from application functions, and controlled upgrades, while acknowledging an ongoing race against AI-driven attackers.
thesis🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumcyber securityNphase
So what: Cybersecurity standards and guardrails will shape procurement of networked grid hardware.
Key near-term enablers for SST adoption are updated UL standards, National Electrical Code changes, first-responder training and lawmaker education, with cyber guardrails built in.
framework🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: mediumUL standardsnational electrical code
So what: Standards-body progress is a trackable leading indicator for SST market timing.
The US grid is roughly 500 GW and needs to grow 2-3x for electrification, and both speakers argue grid modernization with smart power electronics is needed within 5-10 years, with data centers only the leading indicator.
prediction🗣 Ragu Balureconviction: highUS griddata centerselectrification

Why HubSpot’s Co-Founder Is Betting Against the SaaSpocalypse59 min38 insights2026-11-10
▶ Watch on YouTube
HubSpot co-founder/CTO Dharmesh Shah (transcribed 'Dharmmes Sha') argues against the 'SaaS apocalypse': frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic) want to sell tokens through resellers like HubSpot, models are trending toward fungible infrastructure, and chat assistants are the new browser rather than value-capturers. He details HubSpot's AI re-architecture (system of record plus a graph-based 'system of context'), eval-driven model routing, and Uspot, a consumption-priced CRM for one-person businesses riding record US business formation.
Against the SaaS apocalypse · 5Staying off the labs' Yellow Brick Road · 7Labs as token sellers, models as infrastructure · 5Chat assistants as the new browser · 5HubSpot's AI re-architecture · 6Uspot and the solopreneur boom · 4SMB platform-building lessons · 6
Against the SaaS apocalypse 5
Dharmesh Shah argues AI expands rather than shrinks the software opportunity: AI is just software, and it makes a whole new class of previously unsolvable problems addressable, so some SaaS companies will die but the aggregate market gets bigger.
contrarian🗣 Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)conviction: highHubSpotSaaSAI
So what: Supports being selective rather than blanket-short on application software; look for incumbents that can address newly solvable problems.
“in aggregate the opportunity is bigger than we've ever like if you're anywhere near like software have the agency and and are entrepreneurial there's never been a better time to build a software company”
Shah frames the current AI shift as analogous to the cloud transition: some software companies will fail to make the jump just as some failed to move to SaaS/cloud, which he calls the normal circle of life rather than sector-wide extinction.
framework🗣 Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)conviction: highSaaScloud
So what: Expect dispersion within SaaS — winners and losers — rather than uniform multiple compression; pick names by AI-transition execution.
“some software companies will die no doubt just like some software companies did not make the transition into SAS in cloud-based things” ▶ 55:41
HubSpot's original VC pitch thesis was that every P&L line item had a $100B+ software company except marketing, and the internet would turn marketing into a software-shaped problem; Shah now makes the identical argument that AI turns new problem classes into software problems.

Mike Volpi on Why AI Infrastructure Will Outlast the Hype Cycle56 min42 insights2026-11-11
▶ Watch on YouTube
Former Cisco M&A chief Mike Volpi compares the AI build-out to the 1990s internet build-out: AI compute will be fully used and GPU lives are proving longer than modeled, but over-levered neoclouds face a correction while fab capacity remains the governing scarcity. He also argues AI data center networking should move from stat-muxed packet switching to circuit-like architectures (bad for incumbents like Cisco/Broadcom), and draws M&A lessons from Cisco for NVIDIA.
Dot-com bandwidth vs AI build-out · 9GPU useful life and financeability · 5Supply/demand poles: fabs and token routing · 4Systems architecture and chip diversity · 8Data center networking: circuits over packets · 4M&A playbook: Cisco to NVIDIA · 7Cisco 2000 crash lessons · 2Exits and founder advice · 3
Dot-com bandwidth vs AI build-out 9
Mike Volpi argues the AI build-out rhymes with the late-1990s internet build-out: the assets (compute now, fiber then) will be fully utilized, but ownership may change hands through bankruptcies of over-levered builders.
thesis🗣 Mike Volpiconviction: highAI infrastructurefiber opticsCisco
So what: Distinguish asset utility from equity/credit outcomes: the infrastructure survives, but leveraged owners may not — favor senior claims and survivors over levered builders.

prediction🗣 Mike Volpiconviction: highNVIDIAneoclouds
So what: Neocloud credit and equity carry consolidation/default risk; expect distressed asset transfers to stronger operators.

In the dot-com cycle, the players most saddled with debt went bankrupt, but the fiber they financed proved useful later under different operators — Volpi expects a similar pattern for compute.

Fiber bandwidth scaled explosively via WDM (adding colors of light for 40-80x capacity on the same fiber), whereas compute is bound by something like Moore's Law, so compute supply improves more slowly than bandwidth did — reducing the risk of a capacity glut.

So what: Slower supply growth for compute than for 1990s bandwidth supports pricing durability versus the fiber-glut analog.
Volpi believes practical applicability of AI today is higher than that of network bandwidth in the 1990s, evidenced by revenue ramps at Anthropic, OpenAI and open-model inference providers like Fireworks and Together, which grow far faster than dot-com era businesses (though perhaps at lower margins).
thesis🗣 Mike Volpiconviction: highAnthropicOpenAIGoogleFireworksTogether
So what: Real demand-side revenue differentiates this cycle; track AI-lab and inference-provider revenue as the key health metric.

The Neuron Basis: Goodfire's Curt Tigges on Agentic Interp, Monosemanticity & Reverse Engineering115 min38 insights2026-11-10
▶ Watch on YouTube
Goodfire's Curt Tigges argues individual MLP neurons in Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B are far more interpretable than assumed: ~90% of activations can be ablated with minimal loss (recovered by ~100M tokens of fine-tuning), and an LLM 'neuron scientist' agent writes neuron descriptions that recover 74% of ablation damage. The neuron basis beats transcoders for MLPs and MoE experts are topically focused, but ambitious reverse engineering still requires climbing from neurons to circuits.

Neurons as an interpretable basis 8
Goodfire's core thesis (with Nick Camarada) is that individual MLP neurons are far more interpretable than the field assumed: most have one main function, and polysemantic neurons carry a compact, enumerable set of meanings rather than hundreds.
contrarian🗣 Curt Tigges (Goodfire)conviction: highGoodfireNick CamaradaMLP neurons
So what: Challenges the SAE-centric consensus in mechanistic interpretability; favors tooling and labs that work directly in the neuron basis.
“It's usually not like an unbounded number of hundreds and hundreds of meanings that are just like very difficult to understand. Rather it's like a compact set of of meanings.” ▶ 8:28
Neurons got easier to interpret because of better tools (LLM agents that comb activation examples, better circuit tracing) and because modern SwiGLU-style gated MLPs are more interpretable than older ReLU/GELU networks.
causal🗣 Curt Tigges (Goodfire)conviction: mediumSwigloorelujelluneuron scientist
So what: Interpretability progress is now riding frontier-model capability gains; better agents directly translate into more legible models.
Neuron functions are better described as verbs/control-flow gates (sending signals that make the model do something, e.g., recheck, pivot, express more or less confidence) than as nouns that merely detect concepts.
framework🗣 Curt Tigges (Goodfire)conviction: highneuronsreasoning
So what: Suggests steering/monitoring at the neuron level can act on behavior directly, not just read state.
“The neuron is doing something, right? It's not just detecting a thing. It's like sending a signal that is going to induce the model to do something else.” ▶ 1:02:32
A whole class of reasoning-specific neurons controls confidence, 'wait'/recheck behavior, continuing versus pivoting approach, and error detection like off-by-one numbers, and these are steerable.
data_point🗣 Curt Tigges (Goodfire)conviction: mediumreasoning neurons
So what: Reasoning-quality controls may be directly tunable in deployed models, a possible lever for efficiency and reliability products.
Monosemanticity is the wrong frame; the useful question is whether you can elucidate all the things a neuron represents, since apparent polysemanticity (clothing, exercise equipment, dishes) may be one model concept like 'things at a garage sale'.
framework🗣 Curt Tigges (Goodfire)conviction: mediummonossemanticitypolymanticity
So what: Evaluation of interpretability tools should shift from purity metrics to complete, predictive descriptions.
“what if the concept that the model has is things you might find at a garage sale?” ▶ 59:08
Each SwiGLU neuron has effectively two meanings (positive and negative poles) read differently downstream, so Qwen's 5 million neurons express roughly 10 million things.
data_point🗣 Curt Tigges (Goodfire)conviction: highQuinn 3.6Swigloo
So what: Doubles the labeling workload for full-model interpretation but keeps it bounded.
Dual-meaning neurons use context-switching: context pre-activates the right set of downstream readers so, e.g., an 'oral health' versus 'marine wildlife' neuron is read by fully separate reader sets.
causal🗣 Curt Tigges (Goodfire)conviction: mediumSwigloogated MLP
So what: The gated MLP architecture functions as built-in routing logic, which helps explain why it dominates modern LLMs.
Facts are stored in the connections among neurons, not in single neurons, which is how 5 million neurons can encode far more than 5 million facts; a few dozen neurons encode which painters are impressionist, neo-impressionist or post-impressionist.
causal🗣 Curt Tigges (Goodfire)conviction: mediumMLPSpostimpressionism
So what: Knowledge editing or removal must target circuits and communities, not single units.

Cisco Outshift's Vijoy Pandey argues multi-agent systems are now in production (Swisscom, ServiceNow, WebEx) but suffer silent semantic misalignment — three cognitive failures cut a five-agent system's accuracy to 16% — and Cisco is open-sourcing Scope (cognitive observability on OpenTelemetry), Accord (intent alignment) and Concord (negotiation) to fix it. Your Parents’ Wealth Now Matters More Than Your Salary — With Eliza Filby53 min26 insights2026-11-10

Historian Eliza Filby (author of Inheritocracy) and Scott Galloway argue that since 2008 the economy has shifted from wage to wealth, making parental support ('the Bank of Mom and Dad') and inheritance the key determinant of young adults' housing, careers, marriage and city access. They connect this to boomer wealth concentration, longevity-driven elder-care costs eroding inheritances, conditional lifetime gifting and prenups, Gen Z 'financial nihilism' being monetized (prediction markets, OnlyFans, crypto, BNPL), and the widening gender divide.

Multi-strats operate like a hedge fund supermarket with hundreds of pods under a central risk machine; a typical rule is that a 5% loss halves a PM's capital and a further 2.5% loss (7.5% total) gets them closed out and possibly fired.

Illia Polosukhin: AI Is the Front End, Blockchain Is the Back End57 min41 insights2026-11-12
▶ Watch on YouTube
Transformer co-author and Near founder Illia Polosukhin argues AI will become the interface to computing while blockchain becomes the neutral settlement/coordination layer for agents, with Near Intents targeting full-stack agentic commerce (intent, negotiation, escrow, disputes) rather than just payments. He details NEAR value accrual (intents take rates up to 500 bps funding buybacks, compute staking, inflation cut to 1.6%), predicts continuous learning as AI's next breakthrough, and warns AI favors cyber offense, pushing formal verification and post-quantum key rotation.

Lex Fridman Podcast 1 episode(s) · 40 insights

Ukraine War: Putin, Zelenskyy, Trump, Drones and the Future of Warfare | Lex Fridman Podcast #504174 min40 insights2026-11-10
▶ Watch on YouTube
Michael Kofman and Preston Stewart argue 2026 is Ukraine's best year on the ground since 2023 while Russia's infiltration-heavy approach has hit diminishing returns, pushing Moscow toward strategic bombardment of Ukrainian infrastructure. They detail drone-war economics (8-10k FPVs per day per side, 30-40 drones per tank kill), Russian data falsification, Russia's 44%-of-budget war spending, and why they see no near-term peace, with ceasefire risks and a weak US policy stance.

Terence Tao tells Tyler Cowen that AI has moved mathematics from proof scarcity to proof abundance, producing results (including a recent Riemann hypothesis advance) without understanding, unbundling the research paper and forcing an abrupt industrialization of math. In Good Company · Nicolai Tangen 1 episode(s) · 31 insights

Mike Milken: Who Gets Access to Capital? | Podcast | In Good Company39 min31 insights2026-11-11
▶ Watch on YouTube
Mike Milken explains how Depression-era data showed sub-investment-grade debt was overcompensated for risk while sovereigns were the worst credit, how high yield financed MCI, cable, casinos and biotech, and why private credit is essentially public junk debt with 3-5x fees whose real risk is maturity mismatch (SVB, Schwab). He also flags the UAE overtaking the US as top millionaire destination, intra-US migration to Texas/Florida, and health care as the source of over half of global growth.

High-yield credit mispricing history 6
Milken's study of Depression-era credit research showed that lower-quality debt delivered the highest risk-adjusted returns in the 1930s because risk premiums on sub-investment-grade bonds were too large.
data_point🗣 Mike Milkenconviction: highhigh yield bondsnon-investment grade debt
So what: Structural overcompensation for default risk in junk debt is the historical basis for owning high yield through cycles.
“the highest rate of return was the lower quality of the debt you bought. In other words, the risk premiums were too large.” ▶ 3:12
Sovereign debt, then treated as riskless and rated AAA, was historically the worst credit; Venezuela was rated AAA while it had 30% unemployment.
contrarian🗣 Mike Milkenconviction: highsovereign debtVenezuela
So what: Ratings and regulatory 'riskless' treatment of sovereigns can diverge sharply from fundamentals; don't outsource sovereign credit analysis to ratings.
“It also showed that the worst credit in history was sovereign debt.” ▶ 3:28
99.99% of companies in the world are not investment grade, so a market restricted to investment-grade issuers excludes almost all businesses.
data_point🗣 Mike Milkenconviction: highinvestment gradenon-investment grade debt
So what: The addressable market for sub-IG lending (public HY and private credit) is structurally vast.
“99.99% of every company in the world is not investment grade.” ▶ 2:42

So what: Cross-check equity conviction against the capital structure: senior debt of a favoured equity can offer better risk-adjusted exposure.

So what: Crisis-era junk spreads have historically produced outsized recoveries; dislocations are when to buy high yield.

The Lawfare Podcast 1 episode(s) · 21 insights

Lawfare Daily: Anthropic’s Safety Mission vs. Public-Company Pressure53 min21 insights2026-11-10
▶ Watch on YouTube
Harvard Law's Roberto Tallarita (transcribed as 'Telerita') walks through the governance structure in Anthropic's IPO S1: a Delaware public benefit corporation, a multiclass share setup where a single founder class F share carries 50.1% of the vote, and a Long-Term Benefit Trust that appoints 4 of 7 directors. His view is that Anthropic gets an 'A+ in effort' and is sincere, but that weak enforcement, the trust's reliance on the people chosen for it, and a kill switch held by financially motivated constituencies mean corporate governance alone will not protect the safety mission.
Weakness of the PBC balancing duty · 4Anthropic's S1 is unusually candid · 4Multiclass shares and founder control · 4Long-Term Benefit Trust and the swing seat · 3Trustee selection and human factors · 3Kill switch held by financially motivated parties · 3
Weakness of the PBC balancing duty 4
Anthropic's proposed charter requires directors to balance three goals: stockholders' pecuniary interests, the interests of those materially affected by its conduct, and its mission of safe AI for humanity. It gives no weighting, so almost any balance short of putting zero on one factor is legally defensible.
framework🗣 Roberto Tallarita (guest, Harvard Law School)conviction: highAnthropicpublic benefit corporation
So what: Investors should not expect the PBC clause to legally constrain how management trades off profit against safety, because almost any decision can be justified.
“it looks nice on paper, but it's very very difficult and probably impossible to even get a come up with some criteria on how to assess uh whether the balancing is happening” ▶ 12:52
Under Delaware's PBC statute, only shareholders holding at least 2% of the company, or about $2 million of stock, can sue to enforce the public benefit balancing duty. Employees, customers and humanity at large have no standing.
data_point🗣 Kevin Frazier (host) and Roberto Tallaritaconviction: highDelawareAnthropicpublic benefit corporation
So what: Enforcement of the safety mission sits with large holders, such as socially oriented asset managers, so this is a narrow and untested legal channel.
The PBC design is structurally flawed because the only parties who can enforce it, shareholders, care most about the profit prong. The few PBC cases to date involved shareholders complaining that boards cared too little about profits, not cases enforcing the social purpose.
causal🗣 Roberto Tallaritaconviction: highpublic benefit corporationDelaware
So what: Any litigation risk under the PBC is more likely to push Anthropic toward profit than toward safety.
“The only people who can enforce it are most interested in one prong of the balancing.” ▶ 17:22
Oregon's PBC statute lets companies designate third parties who can hold them accountable to their mission. That is a stronger enforcement layer than Delaware's, and Anthropic could gain it by rechartering.
framework🗣 Kevin Frazier (host)conviction: exploratoryOregonDelawareAnthropic
So what: Third-party enforcement is one concrete governance upgrade to watch for among mission-driven AI labs.
Anthropic's S1 is unusually candid 4
Tallarita used AI-assisted text analysis to compare Anthropic's IPO filing with those of other PBCs that went public recently. Anthropic is an outlier both in how creative its governance structure is and in how much of its prospectus it spends warning that the mission may cost shareholders money.
data_point🗣 Roberto Tallaritaconviction: highAnthropicS1public benefit corporation
So what: IPO buyers have been explicitly warned that returns may be sacrificed to the mission, which weakens any later shareholder complaint and may affect valuation.
“They're keep hammering the point that look, we care about social mission, too, and this might mean that you will lose money.” ▶ 19:44
Anthropic's S1 itself names serious potential harms from its technology, including harm to people around the world and to financial systems.

Multiclass shares and founder control 4
Anthropic's IPO structure has four share classes. Class A goes to public investors. Class E goes to employees from 2027. Class F is a single share held by an LLC of the seven founders and carries 50.1% of shareholder votes. Class T goes to the Long-Term Benefit Trust and carries no economic or ordinary voting rights.

So what: Public class A holders cannot outvote the founders on any shareholder vote, so activist or takeover discipline is effectively off the table.
“that single share will have uh 50.1% of the voting power” ▶ 26:54
Founder super-voting control at Anthropic follows the Silicon Valley 'new normal' set by Meta (Zuckerberg) and Alphabet. What is new is giving a separate trust the power to appoint the board.

So what: Index and governance-focused investors who accepted dual-class at Meta and Alphabet face a further layer here: a self-perpetuating outside trust picks the board majority.
In ordinary public companies, the market for corporate control, activist hedge funds and the threat of replacing the board keep directors focused on shareholder value. Anthropic's structure deliberately turns off these mechanisms.

Anthropic's structure includes a 'kill switch' that can strip the trust of its control rights. The founders cannot trigger it alone and need substantial support from employees (class E) or other shareholders.
